items.title: Small molecule structure elucidation from NMR spectra with generative and reasoning models
items.abstract_or_text: Elucidating the structures of unknown small molecules remains a major challenge in chemistry, pharmacology, and drug discovery. While nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is the gold standard for structure elucidation, interpreting spectra remains labor-intensive and requires expert knowledge to navigate the vast space of possible structures. Here, we present an AI system for rapid, automated de novo structure elucidation that combines a molecular generative model with a scientific reasoning agent. Its generative component, ChefNMR2, is an atomic flow-matching model that predicts small-molecule structures from molecular formulae and one-dimensional 1H and 13C NMR spectra. ChefNMR2-Agent augments our generative model with large language models (LLMs) to reason over and refine candidate structures. Across diverse benchmarks, ChefNMR2 substantially outperforms existing tools, offering calibrated confidence estimates and two to three orders of magnitude faster inference than frontier LLMs. We use ChefNMR2-Agent to elucidate the structures of four novel natural products, matching human-chemist accuracy in a fraction of the time. Our work demonstrates how specialized generative models and general-purpose reasoning agents can unite to solve challenging scientific inverse problems and accelerate NMR structure elucidation, thus opening new possibilities for AI-driven small-molecule discovery across diverse disciplines.

items.title: Network-guided identification of candidate biomarkers for COPD-associated comorbidities using deep learning and real-world transcriptomic data
items.abstract_or_text: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) frequently coexists with infections, metabolic disease, cardiovascular disease, inflammatory lung injury and lung cancer. Molecular markers derived by comparing a comorbidity with healthy controls need not identify the transition from an established COPD state to that comorbidity. We therefore developed a two-stage computational strategy that asks a narrower question: which proteins can distinguish COPD samples from samples annotated with a specific COPD-associated comorbidity? First, a Human Protein Network (HPN; 17,302 proteins and 492,195 relationships) was encoded by 20 graph-derived features. A convolutional-neural-network ensemble, termed the functional-distance model (FDM), was trained on known drug-target-indication relationships. Stored training-set predictions yielded an apparent balanced accuracy of 0.811 and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.627; these values describe resubstitution performance and are not an independent estimate of generalization. The COPD-centred network search evaluated 2,645 nearby proteins and retained 224 candidates using a COPD FDM score above 0.50. Candidate expression was then tested in independently assembled public patient-derived transcriptomic data using simple one-feature classifiers and cross-validation. The resulting exploratory panel contained GTF2I for bacterial infection, UBXN7 for type 2 diabetes, LIFR for hypertension, SRGN for lung neoplasm and FGF4 for pneumonitis. Across the saved cross-validation predictions, balanced accuracy ranged from 0.838 to 0.970 and MCC from 0.726 to 0.941. SRGN has direct experimental support in non-small-cell lung cancer, whereas the remaining candidates have varying indirect mechanistic support and should be regarded as hypotheses rather than established disease biomarkers. This work demonstrates an orthogonal discovery framework in which network-based functional prioritization and patient-derived molecular discrimination constrain one another. Its main contribution is methodological: it provides a reusable strategy for generating comorbidity-specific biomarker hypotheses from an index-disease state. Prospective longitudinal cohorts are required before claims of progression prediction or clinical utility can be made.

items.title: DEG: Diffusion-Enhanced GFlowNet for Solving Vehicle Routing Problems
items.abstract_or_text: Traditional neural solvers for solving vehicle routing problems (VRPs) often suffer from limited solution diversity, motivating the development of Generative Flow Network (GFlowNet)-based models. However, the effectiveness of these models is frequently constrained by insufficient flow expansion in high-reward regions, limiting their ability to distribute probability across promising solution routes. Deeper exploration could yield superior results. Diffusion models, in contrast, provide stronger structural guidance for exploration. These two paradigms are naturally complementary: GFlowNet can supply edge-level signals for diffusion to embed, while diffusion can guide broader exploration. Leveraging this synergy, we propose Diffusion-Enhanced GFlowNet (DEG), a novel framework that integrates GFlowNet with a diffusion model to encourage richer flow expansion toward high-reward regions and derive higher-quality solutions. Specifically, DEG exploits GFlowNet's inherent diversity to generate edge-specific backward signals, applies the stochastic noise schedule of diffusion to perturb these signals, and then denoises them within the GFlowNet paradigm. To further improve scalability, we introduce a specialized decoder capable of dynamically adapting to diverse problem scales. Extensive experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets, including instances with up to 10,000 nodes, demonstrate that DEG consistently achieves favorable performance compared to baseline methods.

items.title: HERA: Assessing an Autonomous Agent for Quantum Device Measurement
items.abstract_or_text: Large language model agents have begun to carry out laboratory measurements, but their scientific conclusions are useful only if they hold up under scrutiny. Demonstrating this requires controlled studies because models are stochastic and the context a model is given steers its conclusions. Here we introduce HERA, an autonomous agent designed to carry out cryogenic transport measurements of quantum devices. HERA draws on a knowledge base curated by lab members that holds measurement protocols, software tools, and literature references. We assessed HERA with a blinded trial against an expert on the stacking order of two multilayer graphene devices, an ablation of its knowledge base, and hundreds of offline replays in which models designed the trial's central measurement without running it. HERA's conclusions matched the expert's sealed conclusions on both tested devices. The ablation and the replay studies measured the impact of the knowledge base across different models, showing that with it every model designed better measurements and reasoned more soundly. To test how readily HERA extends to a new problem, we tasked it with finding and characterizing superconductivity in a different material system. This required a few hours of expert time to develop a new experimental protocol, after which HERA did both autonomously. These results show that, with a knowledge base designed for the task, language model agents are capable of sound experimental science.

items.title: Harness engineering enables a multi-agent LLM system to generate cross-domain hypotheses beyond single-investigator reach
items.abstract_or_text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate scientific hypotheses, and a more capable model is widely assumed to drive output quality. We tested this with a biology-focused multi-agent system coupling an LLM to five Model Context Protocol servers exposing 66 external tools. Upgrading the Synthesizer and Critic from Claude Sonnet 4.6 to Opus 4.8 initially appeared to improve quality, count, and reliability. Under a fully matched harness (identical prompts, schema, hypothesis count, and queries), the differences vanished: scores were indistinguishable on an iPSC-reprogramming task and favoured Sonnet 4.6 on a CHO cell-line-engineering task (18.4 vs 17.4; Welch t = 2.89, p < 0.05). The dominant, controllable driver of quality is therefore the prompting harness, not the model tier. We then introduce the ABCD-Stack (contract-gated prompting, diversity-first generation, adversarial refinement, and cross-family evaluation), which builds these properties in as architecture and shifts outputs toward explicitly falsifiable, causally framed hypotheses beyond the reach of a single-domain investigator. The hypotheses are falsifiable by construction but not yet experimentally validated.

items.title: Machine Learning-Based Early Prediction of Neural Microelectrode Lifetime Under Accelerated Aging Conditions
items.abstract_or_text: Objective. Chronically implantable medical devices may require functional lifetimes of decades in order to reduce or eliminate the need for their explantation and replacement, which may involve invasive and sometimes risky surgery. However, when devices become exceptionally long-lived, preclinical studies validating their lifetimes become difficult to execute within reasonable timeframes even when accelerated life testing methods are employed. Computational methods capable of accurately and reliably predicting microelectrode lifetime from early-life data could therefore considerably expedite the development of long-lived implantable devices. Approach. Here, inspired by similar studies predicting functional lifetimes of lithium-ion battery cells from early-life data, we developed a machine learning model based on Elastic Net regression and early-life feature engineering to predict impedance-defined microelectrode lifetimes under accelerated aging conditions and evaluated its predictive performance. We also provide a dataset of electrochemical measurements from aging microelectrodes for public use. Main results. Using measurements collected through Day 5, the 10-feature Elastic Net model achieved a root mean squared error of 3.71 accelerated-aging days and a mean absolute percentage error of 13.90% under device-level validation. In an independent fabrication batch, covariance alignment and calibration using five labeled channels from one device in each target group reduced mean absolute percentage errors from 38.1% to 22.5% for Small electrodes and from 56.6% to 18.2% for Medium electrodes. Significance. These results highlight the potential of machine learning-based approaches to accurately predict neural microelectrode lifetimes from early-life data. Such methods may inform the design of future accelerated life studies, providing meaningful longevity estimates from shorter testing periods and potentially accelerating the development of long-lived implantable devices for clinical use.

items.title: Oxygen drives a rapid, reversible photoprotective switch in photosynthetic antennae
items.abstract_or_text: Oxygen is the archetypal agent of photooxidative damage, and it is generally countered by removing its reactive products or by regulated, energy-costly responses. We show that in photosynthetic light-harvesting complexes, oxygen also drives a rapid, reversible photoprotective switch. Using a new bulk fluorescence method that separates reversible dark states from irreversible photobleaching, together with single-molecule spectroscopy, we find that illumination and oxygen generate a reversible, protein-stabilized charge-separated state comprising oxidized chlorophyll and superoxide. Access to this state increasingly outcompetes irreversible photodamage as excitation intensity falls to physiological levels and is strongly accelerated by ascorbic acid in native thylakoid membranes. These findings identify a constitutive oxygen-dependent photoprotective pathway and suggest that redox-state recovery can determine whether oxygen-associated chemistry protects or damages photoactive systems.

items.title: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins
items.abstract_or_text: An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another's work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally.

items.title: OPERA: OPamp Design by an Expert-Taught Reasoning Agent, from Specifications to Layout
items.abstract_or_text: Analog flows from specifications to a signed-off layout rarely run without manual iteration. Recent large language model (LLM) agents size circuits with optimizer loops over the device dimensions and stop at the schematic. We present OPERA (OPamp design by an Expert-taught Reasoning Agent), in which a general-purpose LLM agent designs CMOS opamps from specifications to post-layout sign-off with open-source tools. First, the designer teaches the agent the gm/ID method: map the specifications to transconductances and minimum currents, choose gm/ID per device role from characterized lookup tables, and size from equations, leaving a few knobs to search and an explainable design. Second, the agent learns the gLayout framework and taught layout practice, and writes a reusable layout generator that closes the layout and extraction loop at designer-approved gates. In SKY130, the agent designed a shared constant-gm bias and six opamps (5T, folded-cascode and telescopic OTAs; Miller, folded-cascode and telescopic two-stage) for fun >= 50 MHz, PM >= 60 degrees, SR 25 V/μs into 1 pF and a minimum dc gain of 30 to 60 dB. All six layouts are DRC-clean and LVS-matched, and their extracted netlists meet every target at all 15 PVT corners ( fun >= 53.7 MHz, PM >= 62.1 degrees, SR >= 27.9 V/μs). The benchmark netlists are released at https://github.com/AMPICLab/AMPICBench.

items.title: EPC-RawDC: Equivariant Physics Constrained 3D Diffusion with Raw Data Consistency for CBCT to CT Image Synthesis
items.abstract_or_text: Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) is widely used for image guided and adaptive radiotherapy, but scatter, noise, reconstruction artifacts, and inaccurate Hounsfield units limit its quantitative use. Recent diffusion approaches for CBCT to CT synthesis remain largely image driven, with limited use of the underlying acquisition physics. We propose EPC-RawDC, a conditional 3D latent diffusion framework that combines volumetric generative modeling with two complementary constraints derived from the same scanner specific CBCT forward model. First, geometry equivariant projection constraint exploits the rotational equivariance of the CBCT forward operator by supervising the synthesized CT through correspondingly transformed reference projections. Second, raw data consistency uses noisy projection measurements of the individual acquisition as scan specific supervision during training. The framework was evaluated on two independent clinical cohorts with distinct scanner geometries and projection sources. For JUST, the physics constraints used measured clinical raw CBCT projections acquired with an Elekta system, whereas for SynthRAD2025 the projection data were simulated from the reference CT using a Varian geometry with Poisson photon statistics. EPC-RawDC achieved an SSIM of 0.97 in both cohorts and improved PSNR over DDPM by 2.66 dB on SynthRAD2025 and 2.10 dB on JUST, while reducing mean MAE by 20.3% and 19.0%, respectively. On SynthRAD2025, projection consistency and equivariant errors were reduced by 55.0% and 41.4% relative to DDPM. These results demonstrate that combining a volumetric diffusion prior with scanner geometry and scan specific projection measurements improves quantitative CBCT to CT synthesis across both simulated and measured projection domains. Code available after publication at https://github.com/ALZAHRAALTALIB/EPC-RawDC.

items.title: LPT: Orchestrating bounded agentic loops for automated protein binder design
items.abstract_or_text: Current large language models (LLMs) can reason over scientific information and use code-based tools, but their training knowledge is broad rather than specialized, can be out of date and is hard to attribute to sources. Furthermore, unconstrained agentic workflows and unlimited tool use can consume large amounts of tokens. Here we present LPT (little protein tiger), a framework for fixed orchestration of LLM stages, each running a bounded agentic loop with custom system prompts and tool access, to enable de novo protein binder design from a single natural language prompt. The LLM stages can query a curated literature database, containing ~14000 papers digested into key findings, enabling recall of specialized information. An LLM with database access answered 41/48 test questions drawn from database key findings correctly, while a model without access answered none. In three end-to-end design campaigns, initiated from a single prompt, LPT autonomously identified the design intent, selected targets, structures and hotspot residues and designed candidate binders to disrupt CALCRL/RAMP1, PD-1/PD-L1 and PVR-TIGIT interactions. Cross-validation with multiple folding models confirms a high in silico success rate at minimal token consumption and low computational costs.

items.title: Task-Dependent Performance of GNNs and Pretrained Models in ADMET Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Structure-based prediction of ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity) properties promises fast, low-cost screening of drug candidates, yet model selection remains unclear because published comparisons of molecular representations often use unmatched tuning budgets and leakage-prone evaluation protocols, producing performance differences that may not reflect model quality. To address this gap, we benchmark graph neural networks (GNNs), frozen pretrained models (ChemBERTa, MolCLR), and fingerprint baselines across six Therapeutics Data Commons ADMET endpoints under scaffold-split evaluation. To make it really fair we gave every model family a matched 50-trial, validation-selected tuning budget and reported the median over ten seeds; architecture and hyperparameter selection use validation data only, with the held-out test split reserved for final performance estimation. Under this fair comparison protocol, no model family dominates and the differences between families fall within the seed-to-seed range on most endpoints. The GNN is clearly best only on Caco-2 permeability (R^2 \approx 0.48), and a controlled ablation shows this advantage comes entirely from auxiliary physicochemical descriptors rather than the graph representation; Morgan fingerprints are competitive on hERG (AUC \approx 0.77) and give the best median on both clearance endpoints, while MolCLR is best on Tox21. For hepatocyte clearance and half-life, all models yield near-zero or negative R^2. No single hyperparameter-optimization strategy, among seven evaluated, consistently outperforms random search at this budget, and we show that selecting the optimizer using test-set performance or reporting only single best-trial runs can substantially inflate a favored model's apparent advantage. Reliable ADMET modeling therefore requires endpoint-specific model selection together with fair, leakage-controlled, seed-averaged evaluation, offering more trustworthy decision support for early-stage drug candidate prioritization.

items.title: Practical Assessment of Agentic Systems in Acoustics
items.abstract_or_text: In engineering, applications of artificial intelligence have so far been largely limited to surrogate models and optimization tasks. Large language models changed this, as they can write software from a task given in words. Placed inside a harness, a system of components that lets it search for information and execute software, such a model becomes an agent that can take over recurring engineering tasks. This work measures how the model and the elements of the harness shape the performance and behavior of the agent in two common acoustic applications. In the first, the agent detects and locates faults in audio recordings from a vehicle interior with near-perfect accuracy. A benchmark on this task shows that a weak model sets a limit that no harness design can overcome, and that design choices take effect only once the model is capable enough to use them. In the second, a case study on the design of a metamaterial unit cell, the agent reliably finds designs that achieve a specified insertion loss over a given frequency range. The results aim to help the reader understand what each element of an agent contributes and how to design an agent for acoustic tasks.

items.title: LLM-Assisted Optimization for Simulation-Based Redesign
items.abstract_or_text: Engineering design frequently involves redesigning a prior solution to adapt to changes in context, such as material prices or system requirements. Redesign often leverages simulators too complex and/or computationally intensive for traditional numerical solvers, which lack engineering knowledge and context, to ensure global solution quality. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret semantic information, including engineering knowledge about the system and changes in context, to help guide search, and recent studies have shown that incorporating this knowledge into optimization can improve search performance. However, how best to combine LLMs with numerical solvers in redesign remains unclear. We develop and test an integrated LLM-optimization approach for redesign and compare three methods for leveraging LLMs (warm start, variable fixing and ReAct) and four black-box solvers (Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, mesh adaptive direct search and random search) on an electric vehicle battery pack cost minimization case study across four types of redesign scenarios. We find that the integrated approach can match feasible design discovery of the numerical-solver baselines with 80% fewer simulator evaluations while tripling the fraction of runs that find near-optimal solutions. We find that the best LLM-solver integration approach and the way the prior solution is leveraged depend on the structure of the design requirement change, and that the benefit of increasing LLM model size grows with the extent to which the LLM controls the search. These results show clear potential for LLMs in redesign tasks for guiding or replacing numerical solvers.

items.title: Spectroscopy-Based Machine Learning to Predict Stem-End Rot in Avocados with the Temporal Effects
items.abstract_or_text: Accurate prediction of postharvest fruit quality is essential for reducing food waste and improving supply chain efficiency. This study investigates the integration of spectral information and temporal dynamics for predicting stem-end rot in avocados using hyperspectral Vis-NIR data. Three modelling approaches were compared: a feedforward neural network using only spectral information, an extended model incorporating storage duration, and a physics-informed neural network (PINN) encoding a first-order kinetic constraint. To evaluate temporal extrapolation, models were trained on samples from early storage stages and tested on day-12 data. Results show that while spectral data provide strong predictive capability, incorporating time as a simple input can lead to overfitting. In contrast, the PINN improves generalization by guiding learning with mechanistic knowledge, achieving the best performance on unseen temporal conditions. These findings highlight the value of combining data-driven and physics-based approaches, offering a promising pathway toward more robust and interpretable models for time-dependent food quality assessment.

items.title: Reinforcement learning for control of partial differential equations
items.abstract_or_text: Controlling dynamical systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs) remains a challenging task in scientific computing, owing to high-dimensional state spaces, distributed actuation, nonlinear dynamics, and stringent real-time constraints. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for synthesizing feedback controllers that adapt to varying operating conditions and can be deployed efficiently in real-time. This review provides a unified perspective on RL and PDE-constrained optimization, and surveys model-free, model-based, and multi-agent RL approaches to PDE control, with particular emphasis on sample efficiency, generalization across parametric variations, and scalability to high-dimensional problems. Two demonstrative examples, the stabilization of a chaotic system and a flow control problem, illustrate the performance and pitfalls of RL agents in practice. Finally, we discuss evaluation and benchmarking practices, current limitations, and open research directions toward reliable, data-efficient, and scalable RL for scientific computing.

items.title: Compile Away Uncertainty: Self-Evolving Agent Skills via Programmatic Compilation
items.abstract_or_text: Self-evolving agent skills enable AI agents to accumulate and refine reusable procedural knowledge from interaction experience without updating model parameters. However, since such skills are typically represented as textual documents and executed through LLM reasoning, even previously learned procedures must be repeatedly interpreted and regenerated, introducing avoidable uncertainty into every execution. In contrast, program execution is deterministic and independently verifiable. Intuitively, transforming well-specified operations into executable programs can reduce reliance on LLM reasoning and, consequently, reduce execution uncertainty. Motivated by this intuition, we introduce SKillCompiler, a self-evolving skill framework that integrates programmatic compilation into the skill evolution process. Specifically, SkillCompiler adopts an executability-aware skill compilation strategy that decomposes skills into fine-grained operations, analyzes their executability, and constructs hybrid skill skeletons that retain LLM reasoning for context-dependent operations while compiling well-specified ones into validated programs. To avoid redundant program synthesis and enable executable knowledge to accumulate across evolving skills, we further design a program asset reuse mechanism that organizes validated programs as reusable assets, retrieves existing implementations whenever applicable, and synthesizes and verifies new programs only when necessary. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks and six model families demonstrate that SkillCompiler consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 32.33\% improvement in task performance.

items.title: When the Same Prompt Gives Different Answers (and the Same Answer Isn't Always Right): A Taxonomy of Failure Mechanisms, Testing, and Mitigation Strategies for LLM-Assisted Evidence Synthesis Read-and-Evaluate Tasks
items.abstract_or_text: LLM read-and-evaluate tasks include study screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and critical appraisal in the evidence synthesis field. These task differ in the amount of LLM interpretation they require. Some tasks involve retrieving relatively simple information, such as an author name, sample size, or publication year. Others require the LLM to read source material, interpret it against predefined criteria, and make a judgement. Researchers should assess whether LLM judgements are accurate, supported by appropriate source evidence, and reproducible under specified conditions. A correct judgement does not necessarily indicate that the underlying evaluation process is reliable. We developed a taxonomy for identifying mechanisms that may compromise these properties and for informing the selection and reporting of appropriate evaluation methods. The taxonomy outlines potential ways that LLM judgments from read-and-evaluate tasks can fail, called TRAILS (Taxonomy of Reliability And Instability in LLM-assisted evidence Synthesis). The TRAILS taxonomy addresses two complementary questions. First, what mechanisms can cause the same read-and-evaluate task to produce different judgements across repeated LLM runs? Second, what mechanisms can systematically affect the judgement or required output in a way that is not apparent from the judgement itself? This study presents 38 mechanisms and identifies the deployment settings in which each can operate, approaches for testing them, and mitigation strategies. We also show why repeatability or accuracy does not rule out a hidden judgement failure and why human evaluation should assess whether a judgement is grounded in the supplied evidence, independent of inappropriate external influence, and produced through a process that can be examined and verified.

items.title: Escape Rooms, Arcades, and a Grain of Salt: Five Original Games for Introductory Chemistry, Built by One Instructor with Generative AI
items.abstract_or_text: Five browser games for a one-semester introductory chemistry course (CHM 1025, Daytona State College) are described: a four-stage retro arcade game on balancing equations, stoichiometry, and Lewis structures; a Halloween escape room on bonding, molecular shape, polarity, and intermolecular forces; a 3D game in which the player shrinks by factors of a thousand from a laboratory bench to the ions in a grain of salt, practicing scale, atomic structure, isotopes, light, and electron configurations; a six-stage arcade game on the textbook's key terms; and a first-week game that sends students to read the syllabus. The games are offered as optional extra credit or for nothing at all; their purpose is to get students to open the chapter one more time and to make the course feel friendlier, not to replace instruction. I built all five in about a month, as side projects; I am a chemist with no programming background and used a generative AI coding assistant, in HTML or in Unity depending on what each concept needs to be seen. Every character, image, sound, and tune is original or used with permission; completion is verified by a code the game issues, so extra credit can be awarded without trusting a screenshot. The games are free, run in any browser with no account, and are published with their source. No learning outcomes are claimed; evaluation is future work.

items.title: Beyond LLM Wrappers: Context Engineering and the Three-Engine Architecture for Reliable Financial AI
items.abstract_or_text: Financial AI systems must support decision-bearing questions involving payments, collections, cash flow, and compliance while ensuring numerical accuracy, traceability, and auditability. Large language models (LLMs) enable natural language interaction but cannot independently guarantee reproducible calculations or evidence-grounded recommendations. We present a production-grounded architecture integrating three components: a financial knowledge graph for enterprise relationships, temporal context, and provenance; a deterministic optimization engine for financial calculations and decisions; and a multi-agent LLM layer for intent interpretation, task orchestration, explanation, and claim validation. A coordination layer, termed context engineering, selects, ranks, composes, and validates query-specific context across ERP systems, tools, and tenants. Based on observations from 15 deployments over approximately 11 months, single-agent pipelines exhibited hallucination rates of about 7-9% (5-10% across query types), including invented invoices and unsupported financial claims. Graph-backed multi-agent validation reduced observed rates to below 1%, although these findings are observational rather than causal. ERP data quality and tenant-specific schemas remained major implementation challenges. Reusable mappings, graph templates, and validation policies coincided with a reduction in deployment time from roughly six to two weeks. We argue that financial context engineering extends beyond text-centric retrieval-augmented generation by requiring structured relationships, temporal validity, exact numerical evidence, access controls, and validation against source records and solver outputs. We outline research challenges in evaluation, reproducibility, privacy, context quality, and cross-tenant generalization.

items.title: Multi-resolution humanness scoring of antibodies via a region-isolated language model
items.abstract_or_text: Antibodies recognized as foreign can elicit anti-drug antibodies that compromise efficacy and safety, making humanness scoring, estimating how human-like a sequence appears, an early, repeated step in antibody development. Widely used scores reduce a variable domain to a single framework-dominated number, leaving the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) grafted during humanization, diversified by generative models weakly supervised and rarely audited. Here we introduce IgScope, a 23-million-parameter antibody language model trained from scratch that scores humanness at chain, IMGT-region, and residue resolution; a region-isolated attention module confines attention to within-region pairs, and chimeric-sequence training supplies region-level supervision. On 2.38 million held-out chains, masking all framework tokens leaves CDR accuracy unchanged, and back-mutated murine residues in human frameworks are detected at 93.4% accuracy. At chain level, IgScope matches the strongest published correlation with clinical anti-drug-antibody incidence (r = 0.567, n = 217) and outperforms a same-protocol recomputation. Region-level scoring exposes what chain-level scoring conceals: antibodies designed de novo by four generative models pass whole-chain humanness (0.966-0.988), while their CDRs score far below natural (P < 1e-30) in every chain class. Quality control turns the same resolution to the mirror-image question: in humanized-mouse platforms, whose domains are human by design, IgScope scores the domain as human and, in HUGO-Nano chimeric VHHs, isolates only the FR2 signal of four camelid hallmark residues deliberately retained to stabilize the VHH. IgScope gives antibody humanization a verified foundation and generative design an audit.

items.title: A Molecular View of the Osmotic Response of Polyelectrolyte Complex Coacervates
items.abstract_or_text: Synthetic polyelectrolyte complex coacervates are a ubiquitous class of liquid–liquid phase-separated (LLPS) systems that closely mimic the dynamic condensates often seen in cellular environments, where macromolecular crowding fundamentally shapes their physicochemical properties and biological function. For synthetic systems, neutral crowding agents, such as poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), enhance coacervation, although the direct impact of osmotic stress on the structural and thermodynamic stability of the dense coacervate phase remains incompletely understood. Here, we utilize coarse-grained molecular simulations alongside systematic experimental studies to reveal the intrinsic compressibility and hydration dynamics of the coacervate phase under controlled osmotic perturbations. This framework establishes quantitative design principles for engineering synthetic condensates with programmable mechanical stability in macro-molecular crowded environments, with direct implications for developing biomimetic organelles that maintain structural integrity within the crowded cellular environment.

items.title: ProtoPure: Literature Mining and Analysis of Protein Purification Protocols at Proteome Scale
items.abstract_or_text: Protein purification is a fundamental step for analyzing individual proteins and protein complexes and identifying interactions with other proteins, DNA, or RNA. A variety of protein purification strategies exist to address desired scale, throughput, and downstream applications. However, selecting an effective experimental procedure remains a largely empirical process that a quick literature review can help guide. Researchers typically survey on the order of a dozen publications for proteins with similar biochemical properties, assessing conditions on a case-by-case basis, leaving no systematic framework for comparison and decision-making at the scale of entire protein families. As protein engineering and design evolve, identifying effective purification conditions remains critical for obtaining sufficient quantities of properly folded and functional proteins. To address this gap, we developed ProtoPure, an LLM-based workflow and database that automates the extraction, standardization and analysis of protein purification conditions from peer-reviewed literature at scale. Given a user-defined UniProt table-enabling flexible selection of proteins by family, organism, or proteome. ProtoPure retrieves associated publications, classifies them based on the presence of purification protocols, and extracts a standardized set of 12 purification parameters (e.g., buffer composition, elution conditions). By transforming dispersed experimental descriptions into a structured resource, ProtoPure makes it possible to compare purification strategies across thousands of proteins. The resulting dataset revealed quantitative convergence toward a limited set of recombinant expression practices, with BL21(DE3)-based systems dominating protein production and recurrent combinations of expression host, inducer, growth medium, and plasmid occurring substantially more frequently than expected by chance. In contrast, downstream purification parameters exhibited greater diversity, revealing a workflow architecture that combines standardized expression infrastructure with more flexible biochemical components.

items.title: Elucidating the Design Space of LM Data Attribution
items.abstract_or_text: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation. We introduce the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT) for fact tracing, in which we fine-tune LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge, providing unambiguous ground truth for attribution. This synthetic setup allows us to systematically alter one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors. With this configurable evaluation, we demonstrate that redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution performance. Rather than proposing a new estimator, we examine two design choices that are underexplored: the loss used to compute gradients and how per-token attribution scores are aggregated into a document score. We find that the true causal evidence within a training document is highly localized, but standard methods dilute this evidence into noise by averaging attribution scores across the entire document. We find that replacing standard cross-entropy loss gradients with the negative log-odds gradients surfaces the critical tokens from other uninformative ones. We can then aggregate only the top token scores to improve ground truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines on our diagnostic benchmark. The negative log-odds correction also generalizes to FTRACE-TREX, improving counterfactual retraining performance for every method we test, by up to 4.9x.

items.title: NEOPIC: A Neural Operator Framework for Particle-based Kinetic Plasma Simulations
items.abstract_or_text: We introduce NEOPIC, a framework for learning the field operator in particle-based methods applied to kinetic plasma simulations. Its key novelty is a neural operator that acts directly on the empirical measure of the particles, rather than on a grid, and is evaluated at the particle positions. No mesh or tree is needed and, unlike grid-based neural operators, no deposition onto a mesh takes place, so the particle noise that dominates the inputs of particle simulations is not aliased. Since it replaces only the field solve, it serves as a plug-and-play field solver for particle-based methods: it can be trained on data from particle-in-cell, particle-in-Fourier or tree codes, and combined with any time integrator, including implicit schemes. We prove that the discrete evaluation coincides with the continuous operator at any number of particles (representation equivalence) and derive an error analysis that separates sampling, learning and time-stepping errors: up to the learning error, NEOPIC has the error structure of standard Monte Carlo particle methods. We show that the particle noise in the training data acts as an implicit regularizer, which gives guidance on the number of training particles in relation to the particle numbers used at inference. A complexity analysis shows that NEOPIC is an O(N_p) method whose constants are set by the architecture alone, independently of any mesh or tree. Numerical experiments on electrostatic benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including Landau damping, two-stream and bump-on-tail instabilities, a cyclotron mini-app and a Penning trap, confirm the theoretical findings. A single model trained on several mini-apps generated by different reference methods captures all of them and remains stable up to twice the training time window, which points towards foundation models for fields in particle-based methods.

items.title: Numerical Integration on Bounded Domains via Learned Reflected Diffusions
items.abstract_or_text: We study high-dimensional integration on bounded convex domains. Given a non-negative integrand r, the goal is to estimate Z=\int_{D}r(x)\,\mathrm dx on D\subset\mathbb R^d. Standard Quasi-Monte Carlo does not adapt its evaluation points to the integrand, while effective importance sampling requires a proposal that captures its concentration. Learned diffusion samplers can supply such a proposal, but existing methods are formulated on \mathbb R^d and do not respect the domain constraint x\in D. We instead build the proposal from reflected dynamics that stay in D by construction. A reflected diffusion progressively transforms the target distribution toward the uniform distribution on D, and a neural score model is trained to reverse this process. A change-of-measure formula for reflected diffusions yields a training objective without additional boundary terms and an unbiased importance-sampling estimator of Z. For non-smooth integrands, where reparameterization gradients may be undefined or uninformative, we derive a REINFORCE estimator of the training gradient using Gaussian proposal densities before reflection, without evaluating reflected transition densities or differentiating r. We evaluate on numerous synthetic targets and real-world problems, demonstrating strong performance of the proposed method, as well as favorable scaling with the dimension of the problem and the number of points used for the Monte Carlo estimate.

items.title: Transformer-inspired architectures make machine-learned electron densities accurate and transferable enough to bypass self-consistency
items.abstract_or_text: We introduce machine learning models that accurately predict the electron density, the central variable of density functional theory. They are built on Transformer-inspired architectures, which require little computation per parameter and can therefore be enlarged at low cost. The proposed models, SwinUNETR-V2 and its attention-free counterpart NeXtUNETR, achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on QM9, with normalized mean absolute errors in the density averaging 0.075% and 0.046%, respectively. The predicted densities are accurate enough to bypass the self-consistent iteration: a single Kohn-Sham step reproduces the self-consistent electronic structure. For NeXtUNETR, the median errors are 0.036 meV in the total energy, 0.65 meV/angstrom in the forces and 1.8 meV in the HOMO-LUMO gap. The forces not only recover the self-consistent minima in geometry optimization but also successfully drive ab initio molecular dynamics. Fine-tuned on small datasets, both networks also transfer accurately to systems containing elements absent from QM9 or larger than its molecules.

items.title: SocialArena: Evaluating Social Intelligence in Large Language Models
items.abstract_or_text: We introduce SocialArena, a benchmark for systematically defining and evaluating the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs). Although LLMs are increasingly deployed in socially interactive applications such as mental health counseling, companionship chatbots, and educational tutoring, existing evaluations remain fragmented focusing on isolated capabilities or single scenarios and evaluation reliability is largely unverified. This work makes three main contributions to address these limitations. (1) We first propose a unified three-tier framework that defines social intelligence along three capability dimensions: role-playing ability, mental state reasoning, and behavioral reasoning. To operationalize this definition, we design a role-playing dialogue paradigm with explicit character thinking for evaluation, enabling simultaneous assessment of these capabilities in a manner that mirrors realistic human interactions. (2) To ensure diversity across social scenarios and thereby prevent evaluation conclusions from being confined to specific scenarios, we introduce the U-TRIMF framework, which guides us in synthesizing social contexts with broad coverage. (3) To obtain reliable evaluation, we invest 132.4K to recruit and train human annotators and adopt a human-annotated arena-style protocol, where annotators compare model responses and provide preference labels along with natural-language critiques. We hope that SocialArena can provide valuable insights and guidance for future LLM improvements.

items.title: Illuminating phage dark matter beyond the reach of structural alignments with PhageFlare
items.abstract_or_text: Many phage proteins remain functionally uncharacterized despite advances in structural-similarity-based annotation. We introduce PhageFlare, a deep learning framework for predicting phage protein functions lacking significant structural matches to annotated references. Across three structure-disjoint benchmarks, where no significant Foldseek match was detected between training and test proteins (E-value thresholds of 10-3, 10-4, and 10-2), PhageFlare achieved macro-averaged F1 scores of 0.871, 0.889, and 0.738 outperforming the strongest baseline (0.789, 0.814, and 0.732). Systematic evaluations demonstrated that protein language model selection critically influences performance, with ESM-C achieving stronger overall performance than ESM-2 and ProtBert. Embedding-guided case studies revealed local structural correspondences among proteins with limited global similarity. Applied to the efam and Metagenomic Gut Virus datasets, PhageFlare annotated 38.0% and 51.8% of proteins unresolved by Foldseek, respectively. Furthermore, PhageFlare identified lysogenic potential in 1,866 prophage-designated genomes misclassified as lytic by BACPHLIP. These results show that PhageFlare complements structural-similarity-based annotation and expands functional discovery across viral dark matter.

items.title: VoroTIDE: Protein domain segmentation through independent hierarchical searches using Voronoi tessellation and physical self-containment
items.abstract_or_text: Protein domains are commonly regarded as structurally separated, functionally relevant, and evolutionarily separable units. Although classification systems may assign different domain boundaries to the same structure, structural separation remains a shared criterion, and many domain parsers assess it through inter-residue distances, contact numbers, or contact densities. However, the Voronoi contact area, which is widely used to study protein-protein interactions and predict contact sites, has seen limited use in domain parsing. There are two potential challenges to this problem. First, unlike in protein-protein interaction, partitions are not known in advance and must be identified before their interface can be evaluated. Second, the contact area depends on fragment size and internal packing, making it difficult to compare candidate partitions. Here, we introduce VoroTIDE (Voronoi-based Two-way Independent Domain Exploration), a domain parser based on all-heavy-atom Voronoi contact areas. By normalizing the contact area for fragment size and internal packing, and incorporating residue hydropathy, we define a pairwise self-containment score F. VoroTIDE applies F in two independent hierarchical searches: top-down recursive splitting until no admissible division remains, and bottom-up merging of secondary-structure elements until the entire structure becomes a single fragment. Intermediate partitions from both searches are ranked by a global partition quality score G, derived on the same principle. On two CATH-ECOD consensus benchmarks, under balanced evaluation, VoroTIDE achieved the strongest performance among all tested criterion-based parsers and was comparable to Chainsaw, the best-performing deep learning method tested. These results show that the Voronoi-based criterion can yield competitive domain parsing.

items.title: Network analysis reveals converging molecular mechanisms in genetic epilepsies
items.abstract_or_text: Background: Rare genetic epilepsies are often difficult to diagnose and treat. They can arise from changes in many different genes, and the molecular basis linking these changes to epilepsy remains poorly understood. This complexity makes it difficult to select effective treatments and develop new therapies, leaving many patients with poorly controlled seizures and reduced quality of life Methods: To address this gap, we first identified epilepsy-associated genes and conducted a network-based analysis of biomolecular interactions in genetic epilepsy to identify converging pathways with high translational relevance and potential therapeutic targets. To run the analysis, we constructed a human brain-specific molecular interaction network by integrating all human pathways from the WikiPathways database. HotNet2 was then applied to identify highly perturbed clusters through evidence-based weight diffusion of EAGs in the human brain network. Results: We identified 2,496 epilepsy-associated genes (EAGs) from multiple resources. These genes encode coding for metabolite interconversion enzymes (20%), transporters (15%), and protein-modifying enzymes (11%). Furthermore, the network analysis identified 19 subnetworks with more than two nodes and 125 unique genes. Gene enrichment analysis revealed convergence of processes including action potential, synaptic function, nervous system development, TOR signaling, cilium organization, DNA repair, and cell fate specification. We identified 44 first-order neighbors connecting the subnetworks. By integrating drug-target interactions from DrugBank using CyTargetLinker, we highlighted potential therapeutic targets within the S4 subnetwork, associated with cerebral cortex development, as well as CREB1, a connector between subnetworks. Conclusion: Network analysis organized heterogeneous epilepsy-associated genes into biologically related subnetworks and generated hypotheses for further research.

items.title: Predicting Pathway Dependency in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma from Hallmark Transcriptomic Features
items.abstract_or_text: Despite frequent pathway activation, targeted molecular therapy remains limited in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), highlighting the need to distinguish activation from dependence. Dependency is functional, context-specific, and coupled; mutations or expression alone cannot establish it. No validated framework identifies tumor pathway dependencies from baseline molecular profiles. We developed a transcriptome-based framework to infer pathway dependency in HNSCC. Nine Elastic Net models used 50 MSigDB Hallmark activity profiles from 953 GDSC cell lines and drug responses pooled across compounds annotated to each pathway. Cross-validated R2 ranged from 0.17 (IGF1R) to 0.48 (P53); leave-one-pathway-out validation retained rank agreement (Spearman {rho} = 0.19-0.56) for pathways with no drug response observed during training. We validated the models using pharmacological, genomic, and proteomic data, then applied them to TCGA-HNSC (n = 565) and GSE65858 (n = 256), examining HPV status, age, stage, tobacco history, and CD8+ infiltration. Seven of nine pathways were higher in HPV+ tumors and replicated directionally in GSE65858. Among TP53-wild-type tumors, HPV remained linked to greater P53 dependency ({beta} = +0.37, q = 0.010); HPV+ tumors also had higher p53 transcriptional activity, suggesting residual p53 function despite E6 expression. The codependency signature had a dominant global axis (PC1 = 62.3% variance; Cronbach's = 0.91), replicated across cohorts (Tucker congruence = 0.996), but largely reflected CD8+ T-cell infiltration ({rho} = 0.80). The framework uses RNA-sequenced bulk tumor cohorts to assess baseline transcriptome-based dependencies and match pathway-directed agents to likely responders before treatment. It is not prognostic.

items.title: Opposing Regulation of Tau Condensation by Phosphorylation Levels and Molecular Chaperone Interactions
items.abstract_or_text: Aggregation of the microtubule-stabilizing protein Tau into insoluble deposits is characteristic for several neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease. While phosphorylated Tau (pTau) appears as a normal post-translational modification, the accumulation of hyperphosphorylated Tau aggregates represents a hallmark of these disorders. The molecular mechanisms involved in the conversion from functional Tau into pathological assemblies are still not elucidated. Here, we identified the role of phosphorylation levels on the phase separation and aggregation behavior of Tau, and how these processes can be counteracted by the molecular chaperone-like Bri2 BRICHOS domain. We found that the phosphorylation pattern modulates Tau fibrillation and enhances its droplet-formation propensity. Remarkably, Bri2 BRICHOS generally shifts Tau phase boundaries, counteracting the dense state, and inhibits Tau fibril formation, irrespectively of the degree of phosphorylation. Solution NMR results pinpointed the binding site of Bri2 BRICHOS on pTau, both in the dilute phase and droplet state, revealing an effect on specific regions and phosphorylated residues, which appear to be crucial for the formation and maintenance of the droplet state. Taken together, this study uncovered the opposing regulatory roles of phosphorylation and the anti-amyloid chaperone Bri2 BRICHOS on biomolecular condensation and fibrillation of Tau, providing detailed insights into the molecular mechanisms involved in tauopathies, which may facilitate future treatment strategies using chaperone-based inhibitors.

items.title: DUET: sequence-only prediction of RNA-small molecule binding sites
items.abstract_or_text: Sequence-only predictors can score RNAs without experimental structures, but continuously updated training pools can reabsorb benchmark chains. Test overlap and within-training redundancy are often handled together, although they affect evaluation differently. DUET combines a relational graph tower with two convolutional sequence towers built on frozen RNA language models. We removed 98 of 388 training and validation records reaching 80% identity to canonical test chains, retained 110 sequence-identical records, and isolated 115 homology components across folds. Across 10 paired seeds, DUET reached 0.240 +/- 0.013 MCC versus 0.192 +/- 0.031 for CoBRA-M3 on the same data (Delta = +0.047; Holm p = 0.0073), with parallel gains in AUC and AUPRC. DUET and GRASSP were statistically indistinguishable on external sets (0.246 versus 0.243 MCC). Real three-dimensional topology improved MCC by +0.037 over shuffled edges and by +0.042 over predicted secondary structure. Increasing the training pool from 80 to 290 records raised DUET by +0.135 MCC. Benchmark evaluation therefore requires separate controls for test overlap and within-training redundancy.

items.title: Ligand-Based Design of Lyn-Selective Type II Kinase Inhibitors by Rational Tail Modification of Imatinib
items.abstract_or_text: Lyn is a tyrosine kinase that plays critical roles in immune signaling and neurodegenerative diseases but is difficult to target selectively because of high homology within the Src-family of kinases. Here, we report ligand-based optimization of the type II inhibitor imatinib through systematic tail modification to enhance Lyn potency and selectivity. This approach yielded potent inhibitors, including compound 22 with low-nanomolar Lyn inhibition and compound 27 with 500-fold selectivity over Hck. Compound 22 showed a limited off-target kinase profile under low-ATP conditions that was further narrowed at 1 mM ATP while retaining submicromolar Lyn inhibition. Complementary 3D-QSAR and Markov state modeling linked tail-region steric features to ligand-dependent activation-loop conformational ensembles. In human microglia, 22 suppressed Aβ-induced Lyn autophosphorylation and increased CD163 high CLEC7A high DAM-like and Aβ-positive DAM-like populations. These findings establish compound 22 as a novel molecular probe for interrogating Lyn catalytic function across diverse disease-relevant contexts.

items.title: Orochi: A Physics-Grounded Python Package for Pair Distribution Function Analysis of Crystalline and Low-Dimensional Materials
items.abstract_or_text: Atomic pair distribution function (PDF) analysis from X-ray total scattering is a powerful methodology for determining atomic structure and arrangements across crystalline, disordered, nanostructured, and low-dimensional materials on both laboratory and synchrotron instruments. Fundamentally, PDF analysis relies on two core pillars—PDF data reduction from one-dimensional (1D) total scattering profiles and real-space structural modeling—often accompanied in rapid-acquisition experiments by upstream two-dimensional (2D) detector image processing. However, conventional workflows remain fragmented across disconnected software tools, forcing researchers to manually combine multiple programs and preventing the simultaneous optimization of measurement reduction parameters and crystal structure parameters that is standard in X-ray Rietveld refinement. Furthermore, mainstream PDF modeling engines rely on legacy physical approximations: they enforce three-dimensional (3D) periodic boundary conditions (requiring artificial vacuum supercells for 2D nanosheets), treat atomic scattering factors as angle-independent constants (causing peak distortions in compounds with large atomic number contrast), and approximate number density baselines using macroscopic bulk volume assumptions. Here, the open-source, pure-Python architecture of Orochi (version 4.0) is presented, implementing physical calculations from scratch in Python (accelerated via Numba) to unify total scattering data reduction, symmetry-aware crystallographic modeling, and real-space PDF simulation alongside a dedicated high-Q 2D detector processing module within a self-contained Python environment. Originally developed for laboratory total scattering studies of pharmaceutical glasses and deployed as compiled executable (β-version) tools at SPring-8 beamlines, Orochi has been completely redesigned around an externalized parameter management core (orochi.base) in which parameters are stored in standardized Python dictionaries and accessed via hierarchical string addresses. By bringing parameters outside the calculation engines rather than locking them inside built-in optimizers, this architecture allows multiple module instances across data reduction and structural modeling to be optimized simultaneously by modern optimization algorithms, machine learning libraries, and autonomous AI agents. For structural simulation, intra-cell atomic pair vectors are decoupled from lattice translation vectors to natively support arbitrary periodic boundary conditions across 3D crystals, 2D nanosheets, 1D nanowires, and 0D clusters. The simulation engine incorporates the full scattering vector (Q) dependence of atomic form factors, enabling accurate modeling of heavy/light-element oxides and permitting direct instrumental calibration using standard CeO2 powder rather than monoatomic nickel substitutes. Furthermore, a sinc-convolution density formulation is established to accurately reproduce baseline ripples arising from finite Qmin cutoffs in nanostructured systems. Complete mathematical formulations for all reduction and simulation algorithms are consolidated to establish a rigorous foundation for automated crystallographic analysis.

items.title: BigFingerprint: A Topology-aware Extended-connectivity Fingerprint for Polymers
items.abstract_or_text: Machine learning-driven polymer design and property prediction require molecular representations that encode not only local chemistry but also the statistically distributed monomer sequences and connectivity patterns and global topology that distinguish polymers from small molecules. Existing fingerprinting workflows often fail to capture global polymer architecture, as well as connectivity across repeat units, end groups, and linking groups. This work develops BigFingerprint, a topology-aware extended-connectivity fingerprint for polymers represented by BigSMILES. BigFingerprint consists of two components, a polymer extended-connectivity fingerprint, p-ECFP, that encodes atom-centered substructures within and across stochastic molecular fragments, and a polymer topology fingerprint, p-TFP, that encodes global architectural features such as block, statistical, graft, star, branched, and network topologies. Through representative structural examples and polymer property prediction tasks, BigFingerprint retains the chemical interpretability of circular fingerprints while extending their applicability to complex polymer architectures. As a critical component of the BigSMILES-centered ecosystem, BigFingerprint integrates local substructural information with global topological descriptors to provide a general and chemically interpretable representation for substructure analysis, similarity

items.title: Diastereoselective synthesis of glycosyl-1-thiophosphates as reporters for nucleotide diphosphate sugar metabolism
items.abstract_or_text: Glycosylation controls key physiological processes such as cell-cell recognition, signal transduction, and protein folding/trafficking within subcellular compartments. Glycans are often assembled by Leloir glycosyltransferase enzymes, which use nucleotide diphosphate monosaccharides (NDP-monosaccharides) as substrates. Cells produce NDP-monosaccharides through metabolic transformation of corresponding glycosyl-1-phosphates (G1Ps). Existing LC-MS-based approaches to study NDP-monosaccharide metabolism in living cells are limited due to the mass degeneracy of the epimeric physiological pyranoses that populate the NDP-monosaccharide pool. Technology that enables tracking of NDP-monosaccharide metabolism from chemically defined metabolic precursors would illuminate these challenging-to-study pathways that are central to immunity, signal transduction, and cellular homeostasis. To circumvent this challenge, we have developed a series of cell-permeable glycosyl-1- thio phosphates (G1TPs) in which a single oxygen atom is replaced with a sulphur atom at the phosphorus centre. This chalcogen substitution generated a mass-unique signature that enabled tracking of select NDP-monosaccharide metabolites. To generate G1TPs, we leveraged a cyclic thiophosphorochloridate reagent to selectively install a 1,3,2-dioxaphospholane group at the anomeric centre of per- O -acetyl-D-pyranoses. Our approach included anomeric stereocontrol, which provided access to both native (α) and non-physiological (β) diastereomers at C1. Next, we leveraged the intrinsic strain of the dioxaphospholane system to efficiently install an S -acetyl-2-thioethyl (SATE) group by direct ring opening with thioacetate. LC-MS analysis confirmed that the resultant per- O -Ac- and SATE-protected G1TPs were cell permeable and could be deprotected to free G1TPs once inside. Importantly, metabolomic analysis revealed that an archetypal G1TP – α-galactosyl-1-thiophosphate – was metabolized to the corresponding NDP-(S)-galactose in cellulo , whereas the β-counterpart was not. Finally, we demonstrated that α-galactosyl-1-thiophosphate G1TP was non-toxic, did not perturb native glycan biosynthesis, and did not impact gene transcription. Combined, these results establish G1TPs as biologically silent reporters for NDP-monosaccharide metabolism.

items.title: Accuracy, Reliability, and Efficiency of a MACE Machine-Learning Interatomic Potential for Aspirin: A Reproducible Benchmark for Molecular Simulation
items.abstract_or_text: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) can reproduce density functional theory (DFT) energies and forces at a small fraction of the computational cost, yet an average benchmark error is an incomplete measure of their reliability in molecular simulation. This study presents a reproducible workflow that assesses prediction accuracy, error heterogeneity, and dynamical stability together, using aspirin (C9H8O4), a widely used pharmaceutical compound, as an initial molecular benchmark en route to metal-containing systems. A MACE equivariant graph neural network potential is trained on the MD17 dataset and deployed for molecular dynamics through the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). Across 210 762 held-out configurations the potential attains a force root-mean-square error of 15.30 meV Å−1, within the published MACE benchmark range, with a validation-to-test generalization gap of 7.6%. Force error correlates positively with configuration energy (Pearson r = 0.51), the carboxyl carbon emerges as the least reliable atomic site, and 90% of force predictions lie within 23.5 meV Å−1 of the DFT reference. Microcanonical simulations conserve total energy and canonical trajectories remain stable, while single-configuration evaluation is approximately four orders of magnitude (a roughly ten-thousand-fold) faster than the corresponding DFT calculation. By combining aggregate accuracy with configuration-and atom-resolved error analysis and explicit dynamical tests, the workflow exposes behavior that a single error metric conceals. The resulting aspirin benchmark establishes a documented baseline for subsequent validation on metal-containing systems and illustrates the value of assessing error distributions and dynamical behavior alongside mean prediction accuracy.

items.title: Fast and accurate neural triage decoding of ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes
items.abstract_or_text: Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have emerged as a promising approach to reducing the substantial physical qubit overhead of quantum error correction, enabling encoding rates exceeding 1/2 in blocks of approximately one thousand physical data qubits. However, their practical implementation requires decoders that combine high accuracy with low latency to keep pace with quantum hardware. Existing decoders of high-rate qLDPC codes can achieve high accuracy but often incur substantial computational latency, whereas neural network decoders have yet to be demonstrated for high-rate qLDPC codes. Here, we introduce neural triage decoding, a framework that uses syndrome consistency to adaptively allocate neural computation. A local neural message-passing network rapidly predicts error corrections, additional iterations reduce residual syndrome violations, and a rarely invoked diversification stage searches for consistent corrections to the remaining shots. We demonstrate that the Triage decoder can decode ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, including lifted-product and Kasai codes, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy comparable to the near optimal algorithmic decoders while reducing decoding latency by approximately one to two orders of magnitude. Our framework is inspired by a rigorous analysis of the exact bitwise marginal decoder, revealing a distance-independent syndrome-inconsistent error floor. In addition, we show the robustness of neural network decoders to mismatched error priors. Our results establish adaptive neural decoding as a promising route towards fast, accurate, and scalable quantum error correction in the near term.

items.title: AegisFlow: Training-Free Non-Myopic Path-Safe Guided Flow Matching
items.abstract_or_text: Pretrained generative models, such as diffusion and flow matching models, have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in synthesizing high-quality data. However, steering their generative trajectories to satisfy strict constraints--such as identity preservation in image editing or obstacle avoidance in robotics--remains fundamentally challenging. While recent training-free guidance methods enforce path-safety, they rely heavily on min-norm controllers that only account for immediate constraint satisfaction. These myopic approaches often yield suboptimal trajectories that hover dangerously close to the boundary, severely restricting the model's ability to optimize toward its target. In this paper, we propose AegisFlow, a training-free, non-myopic path-safe guidance framework that recasts guided generation as a safety-critical optimal control problem with global scope. By integrating a time-varying barrier function directly into the global cost functional, AegisFlow naturally enforces constraints along the entire generative path. To compute the global optimal control, we derive a tractable, mathematically grounded approximation of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that AegisFlow outperforms state-of-the-art methods across text-guided image manipulation and robotic planning, establishing a significantly better trade-off between target alignment and constraint satisfaction. Code is available at https://github.com/LiuKunpeng03/AegisFlow.

items.title: Explainable and Adaptive Machine Learning for Fraud Risk Detection in Bangladesh's Digital Banking Ecosystem
items.abstract_or_text: The rapid expansion of digital banking and mobile financial services creates growing challenges for fraud detection, particularly under severe class imbalance and operational constraints. This study presents an explainable and adaptive machine-learning framework integrating chronological evaluation, leakage-conscious feature engineering, probability calibration, SHAP-based explainability, and adaptive risk prioritization. Experiments use the synthetic PaySim mobile-money benchmark and compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM. XGBoost achieved the strongest fixed-threshold performance, with PR-AUC of 0.5658, ROC-AUC of 0.9068, and F1-score of 0.5369. Platt calibration reduced the test Brier score from 0.1141 to 0.0245, improving probability reliability. SHAP analysis identified temporal, destination-account, transaction-type, and amount features as important model drivers. An adaptive top-1% policy reduced false positives from 192 to 117, but recall declined from 0.4236 to 0.2122, demonstrating a clear alert-capacity trade-off. The results provide a reproducible methodological framework rather than evidence of deployment performance in Bangladesh, since PaySim is synthetic. Validation using governed real-world financial data is therefore an important direction for future research.

items.title: Distilling Large-Scale Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials to Predict Long-Timescale Electrolyte Transport Properties
items.abstract_or_text: Accurately predicting the transport properties of liquid electrolytes is critical for next-generation battery design and requires force fields that are both quantum-mechanically accurate and fast enough for long-timescale simulation. Recent large-scale pretrained machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approach density-functional-theory accuracy, but remain too slow to access the necessary timescales to converge transport properties. We provide a knowledge distillation procedure to transfer the accuracy of a large-scale "teacher" MLIP into fast, system-specific "students", without any additional ab initio data. Our distilled models run ~40x faster, reproduce teacher-predicted structural observables, and produce stable 20 ns trajectories in days, rather than the months the teacher would require. Across a diverse set of sodium- and lithium-ion electrolytes, student-predicted self-diffusivities, ionic conductivities, and shear viscosities track experiment and outperform classical force-field predictions, establishing distillation as a practical route to accurate, long-timescale simulations necessary for high-throughput electrolyte screening.

items.title: Beyond Neural Noise: Critical Dynamics Predict Slower Reaction Times in Adults With and Without ADHD
items.abstract_or_text: Historically, neural variability observed during task was interpreted as noise, assumed to obscure meaningful signal and thus something to be minimized both analytically by researchers and functionally by the brain. Changes to this signal-to-noise ratio have been proposed as a possible neural mechanism behind the increased reaction-time variability (RTV) in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, not all variability is the same - in some cases, variability can have some underlying statistical structure that can be beneficial to information processing. The challenge lies in distinguishing meaningful variability from random noise. The edge-of-synchrony critical point, which describes a system poised between synchronous and asynchronous regimes, could be a good theoretical framework to study these different types of neural variability. In this study, we investigate whether changes in criticality and oscillatory dynamics preceded slower behavioral responses during a bimodal continuous performance task in ADHD. We find evidence that, prior to slower responses, neural dynamics shift toward criticality in both ADHD and control groups, suggesting that increase variability in ADHD and during attention lapses are related to structured variability and not necessarily random noise. Notably, these findings run counter predictions based on the proposed model and previous literature on neural noise in this population, challenging predictions of edge-of-synchrony criticality as a unifying account of neural variability and behavioral performance. Furthermore, this effect did not emerge at the between-subject level, underscoring the limitations of relying on between-subject correlations to infer neural mechanisms.

items.title: Mechanistic insights into coronavirus inhibition by a distinct base-modified adenosine analog targeting the viral polymerase
items.abstract_or_text: Nucleoside analog (NA) inhibitors of viral polymerases are a chemically diverse and prominent class of antivirals, with most agents bearing sugar modifications to induce chain termination. Compounds with a modified base yet natural ribose are comparatively rare and typically incorporated to act as virus mutagens, raising significant safety concerns. How nucleobase modifications interfere with polymerization and the molecular basis of this effect remain poorly understood. We here define the mechanism of 6-ethyl-modified 7-deazaadenosine (EDA), a recently identified coronavirus (CoV) inhibitor that does not induce virus mutagenesis. Its strong activity spans across multiple CoVs and cell models and is dictated by the 6-ethyl substituent, with poor tolerance for smaller, larger or heteroatom-containing substituents. At the level of SARS-CoV-2 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), EDA-triphosphate incorporates as a mimic of ATP but not other NTPs, inducing immediate stalling but also excision by the viral 3'-to-5' exonuclease. While EDA incorporation prevents extension with a second EDA residue, the stalling of natural NTP incorporation is transient and still allows the formation of longer products. A similar phenomenon is observed with template-embedded EDA. Cryo-EM analysis with SARS-CoV-2 RdRp revealed that 3'-terminal EDA is accommodated without distortion of the template:primer duplex, but its 6-ethyl group induces rearrangements in the NTP binding pocket that prevent stable binding of the incoming nucleotide. The mechanistic findings were validated through antiviral studies with SARS-CoV-2 mutants bearing core substitutions in the RdRp or exonuclease. Together, these findings position EDA as a mechanistically distinct base-modified NA prototype that has relevance beyond coronaviruses and underscores the ever-expanding versatility of NA-based polymerase inhibitors.

items.title: Machine Learning-Guided Design of Cu-Based Single-Atom Alloy Nanoclusters for Selective CO2 Electroreduction
items.abstract_or_text: Metal nanoclusters are highly promising for the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (eCO2RR) due to their abundant low-coordination sites and size-dependent electronic properties. Alloying these clusters with isolated transition metal atoms to form Cu-based single-atom alloys (Cu-SAAs) provides a powerful strategy to finely tune their local structures and electronic properties. Because the dopant element identifies and its specific surface site strongly dictate *CO adsorption and subsequent eCO2RR pathways, systematically mapping this combinatorial space is critical. To clarify these effects, we synergistically couple high-throughput density functional theory (DFT) calculations and machine learning (ML) to evaluate *CO adsorption across 1,944 small Cu-SAAs nanocluster candidates. Using reliable DFT-derived adsorption data, we developed an iterative Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model capable of rapidly predicting binding energies by identifying the governing structural and electronic descriptors. Analysis of these large-scale predictions highlights how specific combinations of dopant elements and geometrical sites modulate *CO adsorption strength, directly influencing catalytic trajectories. This work establishes an interpretable, data-driven framework for the rational design of Cu-SAAs nanoclusters tailored for targeted eCO2RR products.
