items.title: Anisotropic Strain Enhances Oxygen Reduction Catalysis in Pt-Based High-Entropy Intermetallics
items.abstract_or_text: The oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) remains a major bottleneck for the efficiency of proton exchange membrane fuel cells. While alloying Pt with 3d transition metals can reduce Pt loading and improve catalytic activity of ORR catalysts, Pt-based solid solutions suffer from reduced activity and stability at Pt fractions below 75-80 at. %. Here, we investigate the role of atomic ordering in multimetallic Pt catalysts by comparing high-entropy solid solutions (HESOSO) and high-entropy intermetallics (HEI) with identical nominal composition, Pt5MnFeCoNiCu. Gas diffusion electrode (GDE) setup measurements at industrially relevant current densities (>1 A cm-2 geo) show that catalysts containing the intermetallic phase outperform solid solution counterparts in both specific and mass activity despite their larger particle sizes. Density functional theory calculations attribute this improvement to anisotropic strain arising from the tetragonal intermetallic lattice, which generates distinct adsorption environments with near-optimal *OH binding energies. These results identify strain anisotropy in ordered multimetallic intermetallics as a promising catalyst design principle for independently tuning adsorption energetics and Pt loading. On-line inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) measurements reveal reduced 3d-metal dissolution in the HEI sample compared to HESOSO sample and binary PtNi reference. Operando X-ray total scattering and pair distribution function analysis further demonstrate that both crystallographic structure and local atomic arrangement are retained during accelerated stress testing, indicating that nanoparticle structural collapse is not the dominant degradation pathway. Instead, the observed activity losses are primarily associated with catalyst-layer degradation and mass transport limitations. Overall, the results identify atomic ordering and strain anisotropy as key parameters for designing low-Pt ORR catalysts with enhanced activity and structural stability under operating conditions.

items.title: Transfer learning on universal interatomic potential embeddings improves generalization in structure-property defect models
items.abstract_or_text: Oxygen vacancy formation energies govern the performance of metal oxides across energy conversion, catalysis, and electronics, yet predicting them accurately without density functional theory calculations for novel chemical systems remains challenging. Here, we show that frozen 256-dimensional embeddings extracted from a pretrained MACE universal machine-learning interatomic potential encode information sufficient to predict vacancy formation energies obtained from density functional theory without requiring supercell construction, vacancy creation, or geometry optimization. A lightweight multilayer perceptron trained on these embeddings (MACE-dGNN) achieves an element-wise cross-validation mean absolute error of 0.38 eV, halving the error of a baseline graph neural network trained from scratch (0.72 eV) and offering a modest advantage over direct MACE relaxation calculations (0.51 eV). Because the embedding approach decouples representation from the prediction task and generalizes well with limited data, it will (1) extend naturally to fine-tuning and prediction of properties (e.g., charged defects) that are inaccessible to generic energy-and force-output interatomic potentials and (2) be trainable on necessarily small datasets, potentially enabling the use of more expensive but accurate tools for generating training data (e.g., hybrid functional calculations) for which training or fine-tuning of interatomic potentials will be difficult. We demonstrate practical impact by revisiting a prior screening of thermochemical water-splitting materials, where improved generalization alters ∼45 % of candidate classifications.

items.title: Intravital single-molecule microscopy reveals protein kinetics in live mammalian tissues
items.abstract_or_text: Quantifying individual protein behavior in living mammalian tissues remains challenging. Here we introduce intravital single-molecule microscopy (iSiMM), an imaging and analysis framework that combines instant structured illumination microscopy guided tissue navigation with highly inclined and laminated optical sheet illumination. In live mice, iSiMM enables single-emitter detection and tracking of endogenously expressed fluorescently tagged proteins at 30 ms per frame. Trajectory-based modeling quantifies diffusion coefficients and model-defined bound and free fractions, while localization-density reconstructions map molecular organization. We illustrate the approach using the actomyosin cytoskeleton, resolving isoform-specific mobility and responses to physiological stimulation and genetic perturbation. Single-molecule detection in pancreas and skeletal muscle, including after in vivo transfection, further demonstrates feasibility across additional tissues and labeling strategies. iSiMM provides a framework for investigating molecular behavior in the physiological context of living mammalian tissues.

items.title: Carrier-Limited Release Risk in Electrospun Nanofibers for Regenerative Endodontics: Constraint Discovery from 25 Formulations
items.abstract_or_text: Regenerative endodontics needs an intracanal carrier that keeps disinfecting across a dressing interval that clinicians schedule at one to four weeks, without harming the stem cells that rebuild the pulp. We ask what one completed 25-formulation electrospinning campaign of poly(vinylpyrrolidone) (PVP) fibers carrying metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, minocycline and Ca(OH)2 can decide, and use machine learning for constraint discovery and decision support rather than as a new predictor. After an audit against the source thesis, logistic regression predicts fine-fiber formation at 96% leave-one-out accuracy, but a one-threshold rule does as well, the gain over the 80% majority baseline is not significant (exact McNemar p = 0.125), and accuracy falls to 84% when mixture loading is encoded per component. Diameter models interpolate within formulation families (ridge MAE 193 nm, 95% CI 96 to 317 nm) and fail across them (R^2 < 0). Because the campaign never measured release, we assemble a same-drug, cross-carrier evidence table: 17 bounded metronidazole and ciprofloxacin observations from seven studies, with two-sided censoring. Water-soluble carriers (PVP, PVA) completed release within 80 h (PVP within 8 h); no water-insoluble monolithic carrier reached 90% within its observation window, releasing 1.5 to 50%; both within-study comparisons separate at matched loading; and blend, core-shell and thick-mat architectures released over 3 to 28 days. The PVP mats therefore carry a carrier-limited release risk, not a proven ceiling, and one dissolution experiment can confirm or overturn it. A censoring-aware screen keeps three necessarily and one possibly nondominated formulation, and fixed-budget replays show that uncertainty sampling finds failed formulations sooner, except the one it is confidently wrong about.

items.title: GLESKit: an MCP-based system for gene-level biomedical investigation and evidence synthesis
items.abstract_or_text: Biomedical investigation at the gene level requires researchers to combine expression data, functional annotations, pathways, interaction networks, genetic associations, drug evidence and literature. Accessing these resources involves databases, analysis tools and scripts that require bioinformatics expertise, complicating the production of clear, reviewable reports. We present GLESKit, a gene centred system that connects these steps through the Model Context Protocol and retains data, analyses, sources and reports within a study workspace. We evaluated report production with 15 author curated GeneReportBench tasks and question answering with a gene level subset of BixBench, a reference biology benchmark for agentic systems. GLESKit completed all 15 reports with a mean committee score of 0.904, although evidence quality varied, and earned positive credit on 35 of 39 scored human BixBench questions with a mean of 0.438. In paired tests, configurations with skills scored 0.145 higher across 20 questions and 0.085 higher across five reports.

items.title: Open Ontology of Polymer Chemistry: Accumulation and Self-Improving Memory Mechanisms for Polymer Research
items.abstract_or_text: Memory systems for AI agents are a valuable component of long-running workflows. They are also a strong form of lock-in for model providers, because the memory system that makes a model better with use may be inaccesible to users. An ideal memory system would accumulate both factual knowledge and the relationships of that knowledge to recurring tasks performed by the researcher. People accumulate particular and general knowledge through experience, the latter often through periodic reflection on what is working and isn’t working at a higher level of abstraction. Here, we introduce an open-source harness for polymer research meant to heuristically mimic (i) knowledge accumulation across research tasks, (ii) the review of new knowledge against existing knowledge, and (iii) performing periodic updates to task-knowledge relationships through reflection. The system, which we call the Open Ontology of Polymer Chemistry (OOPC, pronounced ‘oopsie’), is initialized with a knowledge base consisting of an open-source wikipedia with entries for most known polymers. From this starting point, the knowledge base was enriched by running a 1,092 task campaign across different areas of polymer chemistry, producing 8,899 distinct findings extracted from 1,679 sources on 157 different polymers. GPT-6.1 Sol and Opus 5.5 comparisons were run with and without the accumulated memory from this campaign on 60 held-out tasks with varying overlap in terms of polymer and properties being researched. The performance improvements tracked with research topic similarity to prior work researched from the harness, with token reductions of up to 19% and 48% and web search reductions of up to 80% and 72% (10.3 to 2.1 and 7.6 to 2.1 per answer) for Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, respectively. The harness was tested through five independent restarts of 500 tasks each with reproducible performance gains. An independent review of the performance caught rare contradictory claims and occasionally unsubstantiated claims depending on the underlying model (up to a few percent of all claims by claude on withheld tasks, none by codex). The reflection heuristic was tested as an update to the knowledge ontology after the accumulation period. These updates mainly consisted of extended lists of property names with marginal improvements to finding recall. The roles of review and ontology updates require further study as after knowledge accumulation these tests had little room to show appreciable gains given the consistently strong evidentiary basis for findings within the harness. Looking forward, domain-specific memory systems are likely to be valuable and ideally transferable research artifacts that can be shared at the group, community, and organizational levels.

items.title: Homebrewed SLMs: Autoregressive and Masked Diffusion Language Models Built at Home for Portuguese
items.abstract_or_text: Building a language model of one's own no longer requires a data centre. This tutorial trains one from scratch, tokenizer included, on one consumer GPU, and shows how to tell whether it is good for the tasks of a specialist domain. It proposes no new method. It releases a tested Python package and two notebooks in Brazilian Portuguese with autoregressive and masked diffusion generation on one network, a preregistered comparison protocol, legal tasks built from text alone with a Kneser-Ney floor and public yardsticks, reference numbers for models of 11 to 12M parameters, and a catalogue of defects that only measurement revealed. On Brazilian prose and federal laws, at minutes per run, the autoregressive mode peaks at 64 epochs over the same text and then memorises it, while masked diffusion improves up to 256. At their best points on test, the diffusion bound exceeds the autoregressive likelihood by 0.06 bits per byte, within the preregistered minimum effect. On held-out laws and on acts published after training, the model ties a 6-gram floor in likelihood on the same windows, and it loses to the floor at continuing those acts. It beats the floor at detecting tampered text, and fills cross-references more often than the floor and public models of 160M and 630M parameters, only in decrees, a genre absent from training, where those scorers stay near or below chance, and in filling the blank only when each group weighs the same, since per item it ties the 630M model. On laws, the public models, trained with about 5x10^2 to 10^5 times its compute, lead in tampered text and continuation. The blind human reading is preregistered and not part of this version.

items.title: When Requirements Interact: Scaling Long-Horizon Coding via Interdependent Specifications
items.abstract_or_text: To succeed in real-world long-horizon software development, coding agents must satisfy multi-dimensional task specifications, such as interface compatibility and error handling, and do so without breaking existing dependencies. However, current works lack specification in both quantity and diversity, often emphasizing primary goals while ignoring complex constraints. Synthesizing tasks to bridge this gap presents two challenges: naively adding specifications risks reducing tasks to trivial checklists rather than compelling joint reasoning, and verifying these subtle interactions risks overlooking hidden flaws or rejecting valid alternatives. To address these challenges, we introduce CodeSpecWeave, a framework for synthesizing tasks with rich, interdependent specifications. Grounded in real developer seeds, a synthesis agent iteratively develops both coupled task requirements and executable tests, while a review agent audits solution trajectories from multiple models to guarantee test reliability. Using this pipeline, we construct 4,670 training tasks across 2,865 repositories. Applying Reinforcement learning on these tasks significantly improves performance over the base model on DeepSWE-v1.1, largely outperforming existing baselines. Furthermore, we curate CodeSpecWeave-Bench, a rigorous benchmark comprising 100 tasks and 1,044 specifications, which clearly separates frontier models and reveals significant headroom in handling interdependent engineering constraints.

items.title: Constructive chemical discovery through autonomous reasoning and experiment
items.abstract_or_text: Making a new reaction often requires chemical knowledge that does not yet exist. Self-driving laboratories and language-model agents now plan, run and optimize experiments rapidly, but deciding what to ask next still requires a chemist in the loop Here we report AIChemist, a robotic chemist for what we call constructive chemical discovery. It decides what to ask next from its own results, settles each question by calculation or experiment, and builds the next design on the answer. Given a silyl-radical-relay concept, AIChemist developed an asymmetric three-component silylcyanation: it established that the solvent effect depended on the oxidant formulation and built the next formulation on this finding, raising the yield from 20% to 67% at 88% enantiomeric excess. For an intermediate of the insecticide broflanilide, it designed a photoredox/nickel C–N coupling route free of nitro-group transformations, at lower estimated cost than the conventional route. When the base favoured by calculation performed poorly, it withdrew that premise and rebuilt the search around the reaction medium, where non-polar toluene raised the product's HPLC yield from 43% to 86%. In both cases, each conclusion extended what the system knew and became the starting point for the next. These results demonstrate a framework for autonomous chemical discovery in which chemical understanding and experimental design evolve together within a closed loop.

items.title: IOP-independent treatment for neurodegeneration in glaucoma using optimized ROS-scavenging microparticles for sustained release of erythropoietin
items.abstract_or_text: Glaucoma is a slow-progressing neurodegenerative disease of the optic projection to the brain and a leading cause of blindness worldwide. Current treatments are targeted towards lowering intraocular pressure (IOP), the only known, modifiable risk factor; however, this strategy is ineffective in many patients. An early hallmark of glaucomatous neurodegeneration is increased reactive oxygen species (ROS), representing an alternative opportunity for intervention to halt or slow disease progression. In this work, we optimize a ROS-scavenging copolymer, poly(propylene sulfide-co-ethylene sulfide) (PPSES), for formulation of size-controlled, stabilized, antioxidant microparticles (MPs) for sustained release of the protein erythropoietin (EPO). EPO promotes biological antioxidant defense via activation of NRF2-mediated transcription of antioxidant genes. This MP system overcomes the short half-life of EPO and leverages the combined benefits of bioactive EPO with long-lasting, inherently antioxidant PPSES MPs. The lead EPO-MP formulation preserves neurons in both mouse and non-human primate models of glaucoma through suppression of oxidative stress and optic nerve degeneration. EPO-loaded PPSES MPs represent a translationally relevant therapy for long-term management of glaucoma independent of IOP.

items.title: Parameters for stable Notch-independent Her6 oscillations across a frequency spectrum in neural stem cell populations
items.abstract_or_text: Neural proliferation zones drive strong and persistent growth of the developing vertebrate brain. How Notch signaling and HES/Her transcription factors in vivo maintain stable neural stem cell (NSC) populations during brain growth is not well understood. Genetic evidence revealed Her6, a Notch-independent homolog of mammalian HES1, to be essential for maintenance of zebrafish NSCs. We recombined mNeonGreen into the her6 locus and analyzed temporal Her6-mNG fluorescence profiles in vivo. Her6 is expressed dynamically in all NSCs, with a majority revealing stable oscillation, albeit from cell to cell across a wide frequency range. Her6 oscillates cell-autonomously, unaffected by inhibition of Notch, and is robustly reinitiated after experimental perturbations. Mathematical modelling predicts, and we indeed find in vivo, that Her6 oscillations prevail only when both transcript and protein degradation rate constants are equal. These intrinsic control parameters may have evolved for the Her6 oscillator to contribute to robust maintenance of NSCs.

items.title: Advancing Clinical Genomic Analysis with a Skill-Centred Agent
items.abstract_or_text: Clinical genomic analysis requires experts to integrate evolving guidelines, databases, and computational evidence. As sequencing has become increasingly accessible, this complex and labor-intensive process has become a major bottleneck to the timely use of genomic information in clinical decision-making. To fill this gap, we developed ClinGeX, a large-language-model agent that composes 105 curated executable skills through task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration. On 223 temporally held-out benchmark cases, ClinGeX achieved 71.7\% macro-averaged task-level concordance with expert reference classifications, compared with 45.7\% for the strongest comparator. In a three-condition, counterbalanced human-AI collaboration study, 45 clinical genomic professionals assessed 135 clinically derived cases under routine (no AI assistance), DeepSeek-assisted and ClinGeX-assisted conditions. ClinGeX assistance increased raw case-level concordance across criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making (51.1\%, 57.8\%, 64.4\% versus 15.6\%, 31.1\%, 20.0\% in comparator conditions) and reduced reported interpretation time in all scenarios. During an exploratory one-month real-world non-interventional assessment, 11 experienced professionals submitted feedback on 96 self-selected analysis episodes and reported frequent conclusion adoption and time savings. These findings support executable domain skills as a promising approach to augment specialist genomic interpretation.

items.title: Prefix Executability: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents Beyond Final Success
items.abstract_or_text: Tool-use benchmarks often score agents by final task success, but terminal outcomes can obscure whether the intermediate tool-call trajectory was executable. We propose prefix executability as a trajectory-level evaluation protocol for tool-using agents. The protocol measures whether every prefix of a predicted tool-call sequence remains executable under tool schemas, state preconditions, and data dependencies, and summarizes reliability using Prefix Executability Curves (PEC), First-Error Depth (FED), Trajectory Executability Rate (TER), horizon-normalized AUC-PEC, and Recovery Rate (RR). We instantiate the protocol on stratified samples from BFCL-v3 multi-turn and ToolSandbox, and on the complete Airline/Retail base splits of τ^3-bench. We observe that outcome-only and prefix-level rankings diverge: agents whose execution is conditioned on an unverified plan often achieve higher point-estimate final success than non-plan-conditioned baselines while substantially lowering TER and AUC-PEC. These divergences are precisely the failure modes that prefix executability is designed to expose: they reveal whether apparent success rests on an executable trajectory, where invalidity first enters, and whether success follows recovery from an earlier failure. As a validation intervention, explicit pre-execution plan checking can improve executable-prefix survival while maintaining competitive terminal success. These results show that final success alone is insufficient for evaluating tool-use agents and that prefix-level executability provides an actionable reliability signal for comparing agents, diagnosing failures, and assessing validation mechanisms.

items.title: Rethinking Pre-pretraining
items.abstract_or_text: We report that allocating compute to synthetic pre-pretraining (PPT) never outperforms pure natural-language training in our compute-matched experiments. This holds across four PPT curricula (k-Dyck, neural cellular automata (NCA), declarative reference corpora, and code) and three training regimes: data-constrained, data-unconstrained, and a high token-to-parameter-ratio regime (881M parameters trained on 50B tokens). When natural language is scarce, repeated epochs over a 100M-token corpus beat every synthetic curriculum on natural-language validation loss, with no consistent downstream accuracy advantage from PPT. We find that PPT gains reported in prior work are sensitive to the weight initialization scheme. In an NCA reproduction, we recover a 5.4% perplexity improvement from PPT under the original initialization scheme. An alternative scheme improves both methods, but the no-PPT baseline more, closing the gap between them. However, when PPT receives additional compute rather than a share of the natural-language budget, gains persist at small natural-language budgets even with improved initialization, but disappear by 1B tokens. Finally, models forget what they learn during PPT in subsequent natural-language training; interleaving the same data throughout training prevents forgetting, but does not significantly improve natural-language performance. Our results suggest limited benefits of synthetic pre-pretraining as a distinct training stage and motivate rethinking how such data are used in language model training.
